lessons.title: Introduction and Why It Matters
lessons.body:
When you make metal furniture, the first question you must ask is: will it live outside in the sun and rain, or inside a house? This choice changes everythingâthe metal you pick, the thickness, the paint, the joints, even the screws. In Africa, outdoor furniture faces harsh sun, heavy rain, dust, and sometimes salty air near the coast. Indoor furniture faces less weather but still needs to handle humidity, bumps, and daily use. If you use indoor methods for outdoor furniture, it will rust and fall apart within one rainy season. If you use outdoor-heavy methods for indoor furniture, you waste money and make pieces too heavy to move. This module teaches you the difference so you can build furniture that lasts.

Start by understanding the enemy: rust. Rust happens when iron in steel meets water and oxygen. Outdoor furniture is constantly wet. Indoor furniture only gets occasional spills. So outdoor pieces need galvanised steel, stainless steel, or at least thick coats of rust-proof paint. Indoor pieces can use mild steel with a simple primer and topcoat.

Another key difference is expansion and contraction. Metal grows in heat and shrinks in cold. Outdoor furniture in hot African sun can expand enough to crack welds or loosen bolts. Indoor furniture stays at a more stable temperature. That means outdoor joints need to be flexible or reinforced, while indoor joints can be rigid.

Also think about comfort. Outdoor furniture often has slatted or mesh seats so water drains and air flows. Indoor furniture can have solid cushions and flat surfaces. You will learn to choose the right design for each setting.

Finally, consider cost. Galvanised steel costs more than mild steel, but it saves you from replacing rusty furniture every year. For a business, building furniture that lasts builds your reputation. Customers remember a chair that survived three rainy seasons. So take this module seriouslyâit is the difference between a hobby and a real metal furniture business.

lessons.title: Tools and Materials
lessons.body:
To build both indoor and outdoor metal furniture, you need a basic set of tools. For cutting: an angle grinder with 115mm or 230mm cutting discs, and a hacksaw for small cuts. For welding: a stick welder (arc welder) with 2.5mm or 3.2mm electrodes works well for mild steel; for thinner tubes, a MIG welder is better but costs more. You also need a drill with HSS bits, a wire brush, and clamps. For measuring: a steel tape, a try square, and a spirit level. For finishing: sandpaper (80, 120, 220 grit), paint brushes, and spray cans if you prefer.

Materials differ for indoor and outdoor. For indoor furniture, mild steel square tubes (20mm x 20mm x 1.5mm) are cheap and easy to weld. You can use thin sheets for panels. For outdoor furniture, use galvanised steel tubes (25mm x 25mm x 2mm) or stainless steel if you can afford it. Galvanised steel has a zinc coating that fights rust. If you weld galvanised steel, you must grind away the zinc at the weld area first because the fumes are toxic. Always weld in a well-ventilated area or wear a respirator.

For outdoor furniture, also consider aluminium. It does not rust, but it is softer and needs special welding (TIG) or bolting. Many African workshops use bolted aluminium for outdoor chairs because it is light and corrosion-resistant. For indoor, mild steel is fine.

Fasteners matter too. Use stainless steel bolts and screws for outdoor furniture. Regular steel screws will rust and stain the metal. For indoor, zinc-plated screws are okay. For outdoor cushions, use marine-grade foam and waterproof fabric. For indoor, any foam and fabric will do.

Finally, finishes: outdoor furniture needs a primer made for galvanised metal (like zinc phosphate primer) and a topcoat of enamel or epoxy paint. Indoor furniture can use red oxide primer and enamel paint. Always keep a stock of anti-rust spray for touch-ups.

lessons.title: Step by Step Method
lessons.body:
Step 1: Decide the furniture's location. Ask: will it be under a roof or open sky? If open sky, choose outdoor method. If inside or under a veranda, indoor method is okay. Write this down.

Step 2: Choose your metal. For outdoor: galvanised steel, stainless steel, or aluminium. For indoor: mild steel. Measure and cut your tubes to size using an angle grinder. For a simple outdoor chair, you need: 4 legs (40cm long), 2 side frames (45cm), 2 cross bars (40cm), and a seat frame (40cm x 40cm). For indoor, you can use thinner tubes.

Step 3: Clean and prepare. For galvanised steel, grind off zinc at all weld points. For mild steel, wipe with acetone or thinner to remove oil. Clamp your pieces on a flat surface (a welding table or concrete floor) and check squareness with a try square.

Step 4: Weld or bolt. For outdoor, if using galvanised steel, weld with 2.5mm electrodes at 70-90 amps. Make tack welds first, check alignment, then complete welds. For aluminium, bolt with stainless bolts. For indoor, weld mild steel at 80-100 amps. Let welds cool, then grind smooth.

Step 5: Drill drainage holes. Outdoor furniture must drain water. Drill 6mm holes in the bottom of legs and in seat frames so water does not collect. Indoor furniture does not need this.

Step 6: Finish. For outdoor: apply zinc phosphate primer, then two coats of enamel or epoxy paint. For indoor: apply red oxide primer, then one or two coats of enamel. Let dry between coats.

Step 7: Add cushions or slats. For outdoor, use slats with 10mm gaps for drainage. For indoor, you can use solid panels or cushions. Attach with stainless screws for outdoor, regular screws for indoor.

Step 8: Inspect and test. Spray water on outdoor furniture to check drainage. Sit on it to check stability. Touch up any missed spots with anti-rust paint.

lessons.title: Common Mistakes and Fixes
lessons.body:
Mistake 1: Using mild steel outdoors without protection. Fix: If you already built it, grind off rust, apply rust converter, then zinc phosphate primer and two coats of outdoor enamel. Next time, use galvanised steel or stainless.

Mistake 2: Welding galvanised steel without removing zinc. This creates toxic fumes and weak welds. Fix: Always grind zinc off 2cm around the weld area. Wear a respirator. If you feel dizzy, stop and get fresh air.

Mistake 3: No drainage holes. Water collects in legs and rusts from inside. Fix: Drill 6mm holes at the lowest points. For existing furniture, drill now and spray anti-rust inside.

Mistake 4: Using indoor paint outdoors. Indoor enamel cracks under UV light. Fix: Sand off, apply outdoor-grade paint with UV inhibitors. In Africa, look for paint labelled 'exterior' or 'marine'.

Mistake 5: Over-tightening bolts on outdoor furniture. Metal expands in heat and can crack. Fix: Use nylon lock nuts or spring washers, and leave a small gap for expansion.

Mistake 6: Ignoring humidity indoors. Even indoor furniture in coastal areas rusts. Fix: Use a dehumidifier or apply a clear coat of anti-rust spray every 6 months.

Mistake 7: Mixing metals. Connecting aluminium to steel outdoors causes galvanic corrosion. Fix: Use plastic washers or nylon bushings between different metals.

Mistake 8: Not testing stability. A wobbly chair is dangerous. Fix: Always weld or bolt on a flat surface. After finishing, place on flat ground and adjust leg ends with a grinder if needed.

Mistake 9: Skipping primer. Paint peels off bare metal. Fix: Always prime first. For galvanised, use zinc phosphate primer; for mild steel, red oxide.

Mistake 10: Using wrong screws. Indoor screws rust outdoors and stain. Fix: Replace with stainless steel screws.

lessons.title: Safety and Best Practice
lessons.body:
Safety starts before you pick up a tool. Wear proper gear: safety glasses, welding helmet or goggles, leather gloves, and steel-toe boots. For welding, wear a leather apron and long sleeves. Never weld in shorts or open shoes. In Africa, many workshops are open-air, but you still need protection from sparks and UV rays.

Ventilation is critical. Welding galvanised steel releases zinc fumes that cause metal fume feverâflu-like symptoms. Always weld outdoors or in a well-ventilated shed. If you must weld inside, use a fan to blow fumes away from you and wear a respirator with P100 filters. Never weld near flammable materials like paint, thinner, or wood shavings.

Fire safety: keep a bucket of sand or a fire extinguisher within reach. Sparks can travel far. Clear your work area of dry grass, paper, and cloth. In dry season, be extra careful.

Electrical safety: check your welder's cables for cracks. Do not weld in wet conditions. Use a residual current device (RCD) if available. Ground your welder properly.

Best practices for quality: measure twice, cut once. Use jigs or clamps to keep pieces square. Clean welds with a wire brush after each pass. Let the metal cool naturallyâdo not quench in water, as it can make steel brittle. For outdoor furniture, always test drainage by pouring water on it. For indoor, check for sharp edges and grind them smooth.

Maintenance advice for customers: tell them to rinse outdoor furniture with fresh water monthly if near the coast, and to touch up scratches with anti-rust paint. For indoor, dust with a dry cloth and avoid harsh chemicals.

Finally, keep your workspace organised. Store metal off the ground on wooden pallets. Label your paints and primers. A clean shop is a safe shop.

lessons.title: Practical Exercise
lessons.body:
In this exercise, you will build a simple metal stool that can be adapted for indoor or outdoor use. You will make two versions: one indoor (mild steel, indoor finish) and one outdoor (galvanised steel, outdoor finish). This will teach you the differences hands-on.

Materials for one stool: 4 legs (30cm of 20mm square tube for indoor, 25mm for outdoor), 4 cross bars (30cm), 1 seat frame (30cm x 30cm), and a seat top (wood or metal sheet). For outdoor, use galvanised tube and stainless screws. For indoor, mild steel and zinc-plated screws.

Tools: angle grinder, welder (stick or MIG), drill with 6mm and 8mm bits, clamps, try square, tape measure, wire brush, paint brushes, primer, and topcoat.

Step 1: Cut all pieces. For outdoor, grind zinc off ends. Step 2: Clamp legs and cross bars into a square frame. Weld or bolt. Check with try square. Step 3: Weld seat frame on top. Step 4: For outdoor, drill 6mm drainage holes in bottom of legs and in seat frame. Step 5: Grind welds smooth. Step 6: Clean metal. For indoor: apply red oxide primer, then enamel. For outdoor: apply zinc phosphate primer, then two coats of exterior enamel. Step 7: Attach seat top. For outdoor, use slats with 10mm gaps; for indoor, a solid board. Step 8: Test. Put the indoor stool in a dry room; put the outdoor stool outside in the rain for one week. Check for rust. Touch up any rust spots with anti-rust paint.

After one week, compare: the outdoor stool should show no rust if done correctly. The indoor stool would rust if left outside. Write down what you learned. This exercise takes about 4 hours per stool. When you can build both correctly, you are ready to sell to customers who need furniture for different settings.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Outdoor vs Indoor Furniture

This practical reference is the working document you keep in the workshop. It consolidates the decisions, materials, and treatments that separate a piece of metal furniture that lasts five years outdoors from one that fails in eighteen months. For a metal furniture business in Africa, this distinction is the difference between a one-off sale and a customer who returns with referrals. Outdoor furniture commands higher prices than indoor pieces of similar size, but only if it survives sun, rain, dust, and coastal salt. This lesson gives you the reference data, conversion tables, and checklists to price, build, and guarantee outdoor work confidently.

Reference Data: Material Selection by Environment

Use the table below when quoting a job. The "recommended minimum" column reflects conditions across most African markets: high UV in the Sahel and East Africa, high humidity in West and Central Africa, and salt-laden air along the Indian and Atlantic coastlines. Prices are indicative in USD per kilogram of finished component, based on regional supplier averages.

Table 1: Metal and coating selection by exposure environment
Environment Recommended metal Minimum wall thickness Coating system Indicative cost (USD/kg)
Indoor, dry (offices, homes) Mild steel 1.2 mm 1 primer + 1 enamel 1.20 â 1.80
Indoor, humid (kitchens, laundries) Mild steel or pre-galvanised 1.5 mm 2 primer + 2 enamel 1.60 â 2.20
Outdoor, inland (sun, dust, rain) Hot-dip galvanised steel 2.0 mm Galvanise + 2 epoxy + 2 PU 2.40 â 3.40
Outdoor, coastal (salt spray) Galvanised steel or 304 stainless 2.0 mm (steel) / 1.5 mm (SS) Galvanise + 2 epoxy + 3 PU 3.20 â 6.50
Outdoor, high-rain tropics Galvanised steel or aluminium 2.5 mm (steel) / 2.0 mm (Al) Galvanise + 2 epoxy + 2 PU 3.00 â 5.00

Sources: Galvanizers Association of Southern Africa (GASA) design manual, 2021; SANS 10129:2012 Corrosion protection of steel structures; Kenya Association of Manufacturers, Metal Fabrication Sector Report, 2022.

Reference Data: Treatment and Maintenance Schedule

Coating is not a one-time event. The second table gives you the maintenance intervals to recommend to clients and to build into your after-sales service offer â a recurring revenue stream that most African metal workshops ignore.

Table 2: Coating build-up and maintenance intervals
Coating stage Product type Dry film thickness Inspection interval Touch-up trigger
Surface prep Abrasive blast Sa 2Â½ or acid etch â Before coating Visible rust, oil, or mill scale
Galvanising Hot-dip (batch) 45 â 85 Âµm Every 12 months White rust or bare grey patches
Primer Two-pack epoxy 60 â 80 Âµm per coat Every 12 months Chalking, blistering, or scratches
Topcoat UV-stable polyurethane 50 â 70 Âµm per coat Every 6 months (coastal) Colour fade, chipping, or rust bleed
Fasteners & joints 304/316 stainless, sealed â Every 6 months Loose bolts, water pooling, corrosion

Sources: ISO 12944-5:2019 Paints and varnishes â Corrosion protection of steel structures by protective paint systems; GASA technical note TN-04, 2020; Nigerian Institute of Welding, Fabricator's Handbook, 2021.

â  SAFETY WARNING â GALVANISING AND WELDING FUMES

Never weld, cut, or grind galvanised steel without forced ventilation and a P3-rated respirator. The zinc coating releases zinc oxide fumes that cause "metal fume fever" â flu-like symptoms that can hospitalise a worker within hours. In enclosed African workshops with limited airflow, this risk is severe. Weld outdoors or with extraction, and keep a written fume-control procedure on the wall. Grinding galvanised surfaces also produces zinc dust: wear sealed goggles and gloves, and wash skin immediately.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Confirm exposure: Ask the client exactly where the piece will sit â covered veranda, open garden, or coastal balcony. This single answer sets your metal, thickness, and coating system.
  2. Match wall thickness to load and weather: Never use 1.2 mm tube for outdoor seating or tables; specify 2.0 mm minimum for steel, 1.5 mm for stainless.
  3. Specify galvanising before painting: Hot-dip galvanising gives 20â40 years of barrier protection; paint alone on mild steel gives 1â3 years outdoors in African UV.
  4. Design for drainage: Drill Ã6 mm weep holes at the lowest point of every closed tube section. Trapped water is the number-one cause of internal rust.
  5. Use stainless fasteners and hinges: Mild steel bolts rust first and stain the coating; 304 stainless is the minimum for outdoor work.
  6. Build in a maintenance contract: Offer 6-monthly inspection and touch-up as a paid service. This turns one sale into recurring income.
  7. Document your coating system: Record product brand, number of coats, and dry film thickness on the invoice. This protects you in warranty disputes and builds client trust.
  8. Test before delivery: Water-test the piece, check all joints for movement, and photograph it for your portfolio and warranty file.

Further Reading

  • Galvanizers Association of Southern Africa (GASA) â free design manuals and technical notes on hot-dip galvanising for outdoor steel.
  • ISO 12944-5:2019 â international standard for protective paint systems on steel structures; summary available free via ISO.
  • South African Bureau of Standards (SABS) â SANS 10129 corrosion protection guidance, available through public libraries and trade bodies.
  • International Labour Organization (ILO) â free occupational safety guides on welding fumes and metal fabrication hazards.
  • UN Environment Programme â resource-efficient metalworking and sustainable materials guidance for African SMEs.

This reference is part of the RISE AFRICA Skills course Metal Furniture Making, module Outdoor vs Indoor Furniture. Use it alongside the Practical Exercise lesson to build a costed, warrantied outdoor piece for a real client.

quiz.q: What is the main environmental factor that makes outdoor furniture different from indoor furniture?
quiz.explanation: Outdoor furniture faces weather like sun and rain, which causes rust and expansion.

quiz.q: Which metal is best for outdoor furniture in a coastal area?
quiz.explanation: Stainless steel resists salt and rust best, though galvanised is also good.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid welding galvanised steel without grinding off the zinc?
options: A) It makes the weld too strong
quiz.explanation: Zinc fumes cause metal fume fever, so you must grind zinc off before welding.

quiz.q: What size drainage holes should you drill in outdoor furniture legs?
quiz.explanation: 6mm holes allow water to drain without weakening the leg too much.

quiz.q: Which primer is best for galvanised steel?
quiz.explanation: Zinc phosphate primer adheres well to galvanised surfaces and prevents rust.

quiz.q: What happens to metal outdoors in hot sun?
quiz.explanation: Heat causes metal to expand, which can loosen joints or crack welds.

quiz.q: Which fastener should you use for outdoor furniture?
quiz.explanation: Stainless steel screws resist rust and won't stain the metal.

quiz.q: Why is ventilation important when welding?
options: B) To blow away toxic fumes
quiz.explanation: Welding fumes, especially from galvanised steel, are harmful if inhaled.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when painting outdoor furniture?
quiz.explanation: Indoor paint cracks under UV light; outdoor furniture needs exterior-grade paint.

quiz.q: How often should you touch up outdoor furniture near the coast?
quiz.explanation: Salt air accelerates rust, so monthly rinsing and touch-ups are recommended.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a try square in metal furniture making?
quiz.explanation: A try square ensures your frame is square before welding.

quiz.q: Which welding electrode is suitable for mild steel indoor furniture?
quiz.explanation: 2.5mm electrodes work well for thin tubes at 70-90 amps.

quiz.q: What should you do after welding to clean the joint?
quiz.explanation: Wire brushing removes slag and prepares the surface for paint.

quiz.q: Why is it dangerous to weld near flammable materials?
options: A) Sparks can start a fire
quiz.explanation: Welding sparks can ignite paper, cloth, or solvents.

quiz.q: What type of metal is best for indoor furniture to keep costs low?
quiz.explanation: Mild steel is inexpensive and easy to weld for indoor use.

quiz.q: How can you prevent galvanic corrosion when joining aluminium and steel?
quiz.explanation: Plastic washers or nylon bushings separate dissimilar metals.

quiz.q: What is the recommended gap between slats on outdoor furniture?
quiz.explanation: 10mm gaps allow water to drain and air to circulate.

quiz.q: Why should you not quench hot metal in water?
quiz.explanation: Quenching can harden and embrittle steel, leading to cracks.

quiz.q: What should you do if you feel dizzy while welding galvanised steel?
options: B) Stop and get fresh air
quiz.explanation: Dizziness is a sign of metal fume fever; stop and breathe fresh air.

quiz.q: Which tool is used to check if a surface is level?
quiz.explanation: A spirit level ensures the furniture sits flat without wobbling.

quiz.q: What is a good maintenance tip for indoor metal furniture?
quiz.explanation: Indoor furniture only needs occasional dusting and avoiding harsh chemicals.

quiz.q: Why is it important to test outdoor furniture with water?
quiz.explanation: Water testing reveals if drainage holes work and if water pools.

quiz.q: What type of paint is best for outdoor metal furniture?
quiz.explanation: Exterior enamel resists UV and weather better than indoor paints.

quiz.q: What is the first step before welding any metal?
quiz.explanation: Cleaning removes oil, dirt, and zinc, ensuring a strong weld.

quiz.q: How many coats of paint are recommended for outdoor furniture?
quiz.explanation: Two coats of exterior paint provide better protection against rust.

quiz.q: What is a jig used for?
quiz.explanation: A jig keeps parts aligned during welding for accuracy.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of a poor weld?
quiz.explanation: Slag inclusions weaken the weld and can cause failure.

quiz.q: Why should you store metal off the ground?
quiz.explanation: Ground moisture causes rust; storing on pallets keeps metal dry.

quiz.q: What is the best way to attach a seat top to an outdoor stool?
quiz.explanation: Stainless screws resist rust and hold securely outdoors.

quiz.q: What does UV light do to indoor paint outdoors?
quiz.explanation: UV light degrades indoor paint, causing cracks and peeling.
